newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: BHP STRIKE ACTION TODAY
In Newcastle today, BHP workers will hear of the ACTU's commitment to their future, as strike action spreads to steel plants across Australia.
Workers are protesting against the company's decision to end a six-decade history of steelmaking in Newcastle.
Workers in Victoria stopped work at midnight, at Port Kembla they'll go out today, while workers at Whyala will stop work on Tuesday. BHP says the action is disappointing.

The ACTU's Bill Ludwig says the aim of today's action is simple; to get manufacturers to lean on the Government and convince it to put back tariffs, to ensure manufacturing remains viable in Australia.
BODY FIND ENDS TWO-STATE MAN HUNT
A two-state man hunt has ended, with the discovery yesterday of the body of a man thought to be that of triple killer, Neil William Blandthorn.
A post-mortem is expected to be carried out today on the body found near Maldon, in central-western Victoria.
Police were called to Bells Reef Road in the old gold mining town late yesterday afternoon, after reports of an abandoned vehicle matching a utility police were seeking in relation to the killings.
They'd earlier issued a warrant for the arrest of 47-year-old, Neil William Blandthorn, who was thought to have been driving the vehicle.
Police sealed off roads to nearby houses, before the dog squad found the body of a man in bushland, 500-metres from the abandoned vehicle. A shotgun was beside the body.
OPPOSITION WANTS SAVINGS REBATE TO BE MEANS TESTED
The Federal Opposition says the Government's proposed savings rebate should be means tested.
Shadow Treasurer Gareth Evans says the Coalition has breached another pledge made at the election, when it promised to means test any savings initiative to ensure it targetted the poor.
In its Election Policy document, the Coalition pledged to reduce tax paid on interest earned by up to 25 percent, but phase it out for workers earning more than A$35,000 a year.
But the Government says its 15-per cent tax rebate on savings will apply to everyone.
The Prime Minister yesterday said he would not claim the rebate himself, and challenged the Opposition to do the same.
UNIONS CONCERNED OVER SUPER OPT-OUT
The ACTU says it'll have discussions with some Senators over the Federal Government's budget decisions on superannuation.
Unions have attacked the decision to end compulsory co-payments, and are also angry that very low paid workers will be able to trade away their super.
ACTU President Jennie George says the Government claims the trade-off will be wage rises, but she says there's no guarantee that will be the case.
The Executive of the ACTU will today consider what action to take.
URANIUM REPORT TO BE TABLED TODAY
The Senate committee which has been investigating uranium production in Australia is due to table its report today.
The select committee has been looking at the environmental impact of uranium mining, and health and safety issues in mining and processing.
Committee members have visited the Territory's Ranger mine and South Australia's Roxby Downs, during their investigation.
BACK-BENCHERS UNHAPPY WITH MEDIA OWNERSHIP PLANS
Federal Cabinet appears unlikely to decide on any changes to media ownership laws for at least two weeks, with back-benchers opposing any more lessening of diversity.
Members of a Coalition's back-bench committee on media ownership have told the Communications Minister they won't accept changes that would unduly benefit Kerry Packer or Rupert Murdoch.
Senator Alston Alston is considering scrapping cross ownership laws, which would help Mr Packer take control of the Fairfax Newspaper Group.
The MP's say more foreign ownership would be preferable to a weakening of media diversity.
They're demanding more consultation before Cabinet makes any decisions.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
